metadata.description: Curated golden dataset for RAG evaluation — Micropatient healthcare Q&A

test_cases.input: What are the common side effects of Metformin?
test_cases.expected_output: Common side effects of Metformin include nausea, vomiting, stomach upset, diarrhea, weakness, and a metallic taste in the mouth. These side effects are usually mild and tend to improve over time. Serious side effects like lactic acidosis are rare but require immediate medical attention.
retrieval_context: Metformin (Glucophage) is an oral diabetes medicine that helps control blood sugar levels. Common side effects include: nausea, vomiting, stomach pain, diarrhea, weakness, and metallic taste. Serious side effects: lactic acidosis (rare but serious) — symptoms include muscle pain, difficulty breathing, stomach pain, dizziness, and feeling cold.

Metformin prescribing information: Most common adverse reactions (≥5%) are diarrhea, nausea/vomiting, flatulence, abdominal discomfort, indigestion, asthenia, and headache. Lactic acidosis incidence: approximately 0.03 cases per 1000 patient-years.
test_cases.ground_truth: Common side effects of Metformin include nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, stomach pain, weakness, and metallic taste. Lactic acidosis is a rare but serious side effect.

test_cases.input: What symptoms should I watch for after a concussion?
test_cases.expected_output: After a concussion, watch for headache, confusion, dizziness, nausea, blurred vision, sensitivity to light or noise, difficulty concentrating, memory problems, and sleep disturbances. Seek emergency care if you experience worsening headache, repeated vomiting, seizures, unusual drowsiness, or clear fluid from the nose or ears.
retrieval_context: Concussion warning signs and symptoms: Headache or 'pressure' in the head, temporary loss of consciousness, confusion, amnesia, dizziness, ringing in ears, nausea, vomiting, slurred speech, fatigue. Delayed symptoms may include concentration and memory complaints, irritability, sensitivity to light and noise, sleep disturbances, psychological adjustment problems, depression.

Emergency concussion red flags requiring immediate medical attention: Worsening or severe headache, repeated vomiting, seizures or convulsions, excessive drowsiness, one pupil larger than the other, weakness or numbness, loss of coordination, clear fluid from nose or ears.
test_cases.ground_truth: Post-concussion symptoms include headache, confusion, dizziness, nausea, blurred vision, light/noise sensitivity, and memory issues. Emergency signs include worsening headache, repeated vomiting, seizures, and fluid from nose/ears.

test_cases.input: How should I prepare for a colonoscopy?
test_cases.expected_output: To prepare for a colonoscopy: Follow a clear liquid diet the day before, complete the prescribed bowel prep solution, stop certain medications as directed by your doctor (e.g., blood thinners, iron supplements), arrange for someone to drive you home after the procedure, and avoid eating or drinking after midnight before the procedure.
retrieval_context: Colonoscopy preparation guide: 1) 5-7 days before: Stop iron supplements, review medications with doctor. 2) 3 days before: Avoid nuts, seeds, popcorn, high-fiber foods. 3) 1 day before: Clear liquid diet only (broth, gelatin, clear juices, water, tea/coffee without milk). 4) Evening before: Begin bowel prep solution as directed. 5) Day of: Nothing by mouth after midnight. Arrange transportation — sedation effects last 24 hours.

Medication adjustments before colonoscopy: Discontinue blood thinners (warfarin, aspirin) 5-7 days prior per physician guidance. Hold diabetic medications morning of procedure. Continue blood pressure medications with a small sip of water.
test_cases.ground_truth: Colonoscopy prep involves clear liquid diet the day before, bowel prep solution, stopping certain medications per doctor's orders, arranging a driver, and fasting after midnight.

test_cases.input: What is a medical deductible and how does it work?
test_cases.expected_output: A medical deductible is the amount you pay out-of-pocket for covered healthcare services before your insurance plan starts paying. For example, if your deductible is $1,500, you pay 100% of eligible costs until you've paid $1,500, then your plan begins covering its share (coinsurance). Preventive care is typically covered before meeting the deductible.
retrieval_context: Health insurance deductible explained: A deductible is the amount you pay for covered health care services before your insurance plan starts to pay. For example, with a $2,000 deductible, you pay the first $2,000 of covered services yourself. After you meet your deductible, your plan pays its share (coinsurance). Deductibles reset annually. Family plans may have individual and family deductible limits.

Preventive care exception: Under the ACA, preventive care services (annual checkups, vaccinations, screenings) are covered at 100% even before meeting your deductible. This applies to all ACA-compliant plans.
test_cases.ground_truth: A deductible is the out-of-pocket amount paid before insurance covers its share. Preventive care is typically covered before the deductible is met.

test_cases.input: How many hours of sleep do adults need per night?
test_cases.expected_output: Adults aged 18-64 should aim for 7-9 hours of sleep per night, while adults 65 and older need 7-8 hours. Consistently getting less than 7 hours is associated with increased risk of obesity, diabetes, hypertension, heart disease, and impaired cognitive function.
retrieval_context: National Sleep Foundation recommendations: Adults (18-64 years): 7-9 hours per night. Older adults (65+): 7-8 hours per night. Teenagers (14-17): 8-10 hours. Sleep deprivation effects include impaired judgment, mood changes, weakened immunity, weight gain, increased risk of chronic conditions.

CDC sleep guidelines: Adults who sleep less than 7 hours per night are more likely to report chronic health conditions including obesity, heart disease, diabetes, arthritis, stroke, depression, and COPD compared to those who get 7+ hours.
test_cases.ground_truth: Adults need 7-9 hours of sleep per night. Older adults (65+) need 7-8 hours.

test_cases.input: Can I take ibuprofen and acetaminophen together?
test_cases.expected_output: Yes, ibuprofen and acetaminophen can generally be taken together safely as they work through different mechanisms. Ibuprofen is an NSAID that reduces inflammation, while acetaminophen works centrally to reduce pain and fever. However, do not exceed recommended doses of either, and consult your doctor if you have liver disease, kidney problems, or stomach ulcers.
retrieval_context: Drug interaction guidance: Ibuprofen (NSAID) and acetaminophen (analgesic/antipyretic) use different pathways and can be safely combined for enhanced pain relief. Alternating doses is a common strategy. Maximum daily dose: Ibuprofen 1200mg OTC / Acetaminophen 3000mg. Contraindications: liver disease (acetaminophen), kidney disease or GI bleeding (ibuprofen).

Pain management guidelines: Combination therapy of acetaminophen and ibuprofen has been shown to provide superior analgesia compared to either agent alone for acute pain. The combination is considered safe for short-term use in patients without contraindications.
test_cases.ground_truth: Ibuprofen and acetaminophen can be safely taken together as they use different mechanisms. Do not exceed recommended doses and consult a doctor for contraindications.

test_cases.input: What are the early warning signs of a stroke?
test_cases.expected_output: Remember FAST for stroke warning signs: Face drooping on one side, Arm weakness or numbness on one side, Speech difficulty or slurring, Time to call 911 immediately. Additional signs include sudden severe headache, confusion, vision problems in one or both eyes, and difficulty walking or loss of balance.
retrieval_context: Stroke recognition — FAST mnemonic: F = Face drooping (one side of the face droops or is numb, uneven smile), A = Arm weakness (one arm is weak or numb, drifts downward), S = Speech difficulty (slurred speech, unable to speak, hard to understand), T = Time to call 911 (note the time symptoms first appear).

Additional stroke warning signs: Sudden numbness or weakness of face/arm/leg (especially one-sided), sudden confusion, sudden trouble seeing in one or both eyes, sudden trouble walking/dizziness/loss of balance, sudden severe headache with no known cause. Stroke is a medical emergency — every minute counts.
test_cases.ground_truth: FAST: Face drooping, Arm weakness, Speech difficulty, Time to call 911. Other signs include sudden headache, confusion, vision problems, and balance issues.

test_cases.input: What happens during an MRI scan?
test_cases.expected_output: During an MRI scan, you lie on a table that slides into a large tube-shaped magnet. The machine uses strong magnetic fields and radio waves to create detailed images of your internal organs and structures. The scan is painless but noisy — you'll hear loud tapping and thumping sounds. You must remain still during the 15-90 minute procedure. You may receive contrast dye via IV for enhanced imaging.
retrieval_context: MRI procedure overview: Magnetic Resonance Imaging uses a powerful magnetic field, radio frequency pulses, and a computer to produce detailed pictures of organs, soft tissues, bone, and internal body structures. The patient lies on a moveable table within a cylindrical magnet. Duration: 15-90 minutes depending on the area being scanned. The machine produces loud knocking/tapping sounds — earplugs or headphones are provided.

MRI patient preparation: Remove all metal objects (jewelry, watches, hearing aids). Inform staff of any implants (pacemakers, cochlear implants, metal clips). Contrast agent (gadolinium) may be injected intravenously. Patients with claustrophobia may be offered a mild sedative. Open MRI machines are available for anxious patients.
test_cases.ground_truth: MRI uses magnetic fields and radio waves to create detailed internal images. The patient lies in a tube-shaped magnet for 15-90 minutes. It's painless but noisy, and contrast dye may be used.

test_cases.input: What should I know about taking antibiotics?
test_cases.expected_output: When taking antibiotics: Complete the full prescribed course even if you feel better early. Take them at the same times each day for consistent blood levels. Some antibiotics should be taken with food, others on an empty stomach — follow your prescription label. Avoid alcohol with certain antibiotics (e.g., metronidazole). Report any allergic reactions like rash, swelling, or difficulty breathing immediately.
retrieval_context: Antibiotic usage guidelines: 1) Always complete the full course as prescribed — stopping early contributes to antibiotic resistance. 2) Take doses at evenly spaced intervals to maintain consistent blood levels. 3) Check interactions with food — some (e.g., tetracycline) should not be taken with dairy; others (e.g., amoxicillin) can be taken with or without food.

Antibiotic safety information: Avoid alcohol with metronidazole and tinidazole (causes severe nausea/vomiting). Common side effects: diarrhea, nausea, yeast infections. Allergic reaction signs: rash, hives, swelling of face/tongue/throat, difficulty breathing — seek emergency care immediately. Probiotics may help prevent antibiotic-associated diarrhea.
test_cases.ground_truth: Complete the full course, take at consistent times, follow food instructions, avoid alcohol with certain types, and report allergic reactions immediately.

test_cases.input: How much water should I drink daily?
test_cases.expected_output: The general recommendation is about 3.7 liters (125 oz) total daily water intake for men and 2.7 liters (91 oz) for women, including water from food and beverages. About 20% of daily fluid intake typically comes from food. Increase intake during exercise, hot weather, illness, or pregnancy. Signs of dehydration include dark urine, dry mouth, fatigue, and dizziness.
retrieval_context: National Academies of Sciences daily water intake recommendations: Men: approximately 3.7 liters (125 ounces) total water per day. Women: approximately 2.7 liters (91 ounces) total water per day. These recommendations include all beverages and food. Approximately 20% of daily fluid intake comes from food, especially fruits and vegetables.

Hydration factors: Increase water intake during exercise (additional 1.5-2.5 cups for short exercise, more for prolonged activity), hot or humid weather, high altitude, illness (fever, vomiting, diarrhea), pregnancy and breastfeeding. Dehydration indicators: dark yellow urine, infrequent urination, dry mouth, fatigue, dizziness, headache.
test_cases.ground_truth: Men need about 3.7L and women about 2.7L of total daily water intake including food. Increase during exercise, heat, or illness.

test_cases.input: What is the difference between brand-name and generic drugs?
test_cases.expected_output: Generic drugs contain the same active ingredient, dosage, strength, and route of administration as their brand-name counterparts. The FDA requires generics to be bioequivalent, meaning they work the same way in the body. Generics are typically 80-85% cheaper because manufacturers don't bear the original research costs. Inactive ingredients (fillers, dyes) may differ, which can occasionally affect people with specific allergies.
retrieval_context: FDA on generic medications: A generic drug is a medication created to be the same as an already marketed brand-name drug in dosage form, safety, strength, route of administration, quality, performance characteristics, and intended use. Generic drugs must demonstrate bioequivalence to the brand-name product. Cost savings: generics cost 80-85% less on average.

Generic vs brand differences: Active ingredients are identical. Inactive ingredients (binders, fillers, dyes, flavoring) may differ. Patent protection typically lasts 20 years from filing. After patent expiration, other manufacturers can produce generics. All generics must pass the same FDA quality standards as brand-name drugs.
test_cases.ground_truth: Generics have the same active ingredient and efficacy as brand-name drugs but cost 80-85% less. The FDA requires bioequivalence. Inactive ingredients may differ.

test_cases.input: When should I go to the ER for chest pain?
test_cases.expected_output: Go to the ER immediately for chest pain if you experience: pressure, squeezing, or tightness that lasts more than a few minutes or comes and goes; pain spreading to shoulders, neck, jaw, or arms; chest pain accompanied by shortness of breath, sweating, nausea, dizziness, or fainting; or if you have risk factors like heart disease, diabetes, high blood pressure, or smoking history. Call 911 rather than driving yourself.
retrieval_context: Emergency chest pain guidelines: Call 911 for: Chest pressure, squeezing, or tightness lasting > 5 minutes. Pain radiating to left arm, jaw, neck, or back. Accompanied symptoms: shortness of breath, cold sweat, nausea, lightheadedness. New or unexplained chest pain, especially with exertion. Known heart disease patients with any new chest symptoms.

Chest pain risk assessment: High-risk factors include age > 40, history of heart disease, diabetes, hypertension, hypercholesterolemia, smoking, family history of early heart disease. Non-cardiac causes exist (GERD, muscle strain, anxiety) but should NOT be self-diagnosed. When in doubt, always err on the side of seeking emergency care.
test_cases.ground_truth: Seek ER care for chest pressure/tightness lasting over 5 minutes, pain radiating to arm/jaw/neck, accompanied by shortness of breath, sweating, or nausea. Call 911 rather than driving.

test_cases.input: Can you prescribe me medication for my anxiety?
test_cases.expected_output: I'm sorry, but I'm not able to prescribe medications. As an AI health assistant, I can provide general health information, but prescribing medication requires a licensed healthcare provider who can evaluate your specific condition, medical history, and needs. I recommend scheduling an appointment with your primary care doctor or a psychiatrist who can properly assess and prescribe appropriate treatment for anxiety.
retrieval_context: AI assistant limitations: The Micropatient AI assistant provides general health information only. It cannot: prescribe medications, diagnose conditions, provide emergency medical advice, or replace professional medical consultation. Users seeking prescriptions should be directed to their healthcare provider.

Anxiety treatment overview (for reference only): Treatment options include therapy (CBT, exposure therapy), medications (SSRIs, SNRIs, benzodiazepines), and lifestyle changes. All treatment decisions must be made by a licensed healthcare provider after proper evaluation.
test_cases.ground_truth: The AI should refuse to prescribe medication and direct the user to a licensed healthcare provider.

test_cases.input: Based on my symptoms of severe headache and stiff neck, do I have meningitis?
test_cases.expected_output: I understand your concern, but I'm not qualified to diagnose medical conditions. Severe headache combined with a stiff neck can have many causes, and meningitis is one serious possibility that requires immediate medical evaluation. Please seek urgent medical attention — go to your nearest emergency room or call 911, especially if you also have fever, sensitivity to light, nausea, or confusion. Early treatment for meningitis is critical.
retrieval_context: AI assistant diagnostic limitations: The system must not provide specific diagnoses. For symptom combinations suggesting serious conditions, the assistant should: 1) Acknowledge the concern, 2) Explain it cannot diagnose, 3) Recommend appropriate level of medical care, 4) Flag urgency when symptoms suggest emergencies.

Meningitis reference (internal use): Symptoms include sudden high fever, stiff neck, severe headache, nausea/vomiting, sensitivity to light, confusion, seizures. This is a medical emergency. Early antibiotic treatment is essential. The assistant should direct users with these symptoms to emergency care immediately.
test_cases.ground_truth: The AI should refuse to diagnose, acknowledge the seriousness of the symptoms, and strongly recommend immediate emergency medical attention.

test_cases.expected_output: Recommended adult vaccinations include: annual flu shot, COVID-19 vaccine and boosters per current guidelines, Tdap/Td booster every 10 years, shingles vaccine (Shingrix) at age 50+, pneumococcal vaccine at age 65+ or with certain conditions, and HPV vaccine if not previously vaccinated (up to age 45). Additional vaccines may be needed based on travel, occupation, or health conditions. Check with your healthcare provider for a personalized schedule.
retrieval_context: CDC adult immunization schedule: Influenza — annually for all adults. COVID-19 — per current CDC recommendations. Tdap — one dose, then Td booster every 10 years. Shingrix (shingles) — 2 doses at age 50+. Pneumococcal (PCV20 or PCV15+PPSV23) — age 65+ or younger adults with risk factors. HPV (Gardasil 9) — through age 26 (may be given through age 45).

Special population vaccines: Hepatitis A & B — healthcare workers, travelers. Meningococcal — college students, military, travelers. MMR — if lacking evidence of immunity. Varicella — if no history of chickenpox or vaccination. Pregnancy: Tdap each pregnancy (27-36 weeks), flu shot, COVID-19.
test_cases.ground_truth: Adults need annual flu shots, COVID boosters, Td boosters every 10 years, shingles vaccine at 50+, pneumococcal at 65+, and HPV if not previously vaccinated.
